title: Diplopia Decoded: Monocular vs. Binocular Vision
summary: Diplopia, or double vision, is a critical symptom requiring thorough ophthalmic and systemic evaluation. This comprehensive guide dissects the etiologies, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and management strategies for both monocular and binocular diplopia, crucial for ophthalmology residents and practitioners.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Diplopia, commonly known as double vision, is the perception of two images of a single object. It is a symptom, not a diagnosis, indicating an underlying issue with visual processing. Differentiating between monocular and binocular diplopia is the crucial first step in diagnosis, guiding the subsequent workup and management.

rows: Persists when affected eye is open, disappears when affected eye is closed
Disappears when either eye is closed
Typically slight offset (ghosting), vertical/horizontal/oblique, often overlapping
Distinct separation of images, horizontal/vertical/oblique, can be crossed or uncrossed
Ocular misalignment (between two eyes) or neurological disruption of fusion

content.description: Prevalence (%) of diplopia in the general adult population, showing that both types are relatively common, though specific etiologies vary widely by age and systemic health. (Approximate figures for illustration).

branches: Corneal Irregularities: Astigmatism (uncorrected/irregular), Keratoconus, Pterygium, Corneal scarring/dystrophy (e.g., Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy), Dry eye disease

Lenticular Issues: Cataract (especially early cortical or nuclear sclerotic), Lens subluxation/dislocation, Polycoria, Intraocular lens (IOL) decentration/tilt/edge glare, Posterior capsular opacification
Retinal Pathology: Epiretinal membrane, Macular edema (e.g., diabetic, RVO), Central serous chorioretinopathy, Foveal schisis, Macular hole (less common)
Refractive Errors: High uncorrected astigmatism, Presbyopia (unusual), Anisometropia with poor correction
Neurological (rare): Cortical polyopia (higher-order processing deficit, usually transient)

Neurogenic: Cranial Neuropathies (CN III, IV, VI palsies due to microvascular ischemia, compression, inflammation, trauma), Myasthenia Gravis (fluctuating), Botulism, Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO), Supranuclear Lesions (e.g., progressive supranuclear palsy, rare), Brainstem Lesions (stroke, tumor, demyelination)

Restrictive: Thyroid Eye Disease (Graves' Ophthalmopathy - inferior/medial rectus restriction), Orbital Pseudotumor, Orbital Trauma (blow-out fracture with muscle entrapment), Orbital Masses (tumor, inflammation), Duane's Retraction Syndrome, Brown's Syndrome
Mechanical: Orbital Masses displacing the globe, Scarring from prior surgery or trauma, Large globe (e.g., high myopia) leading to mechanical restriction
Decompensated Strabismus: Long-standing phoria or intermittent tropia that becomes manifest and symptomatic, often due to systemic illness, fatigue, or age-related decompensation.

sections.title: 6. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Monocular Diplopia: Often described as ghosting, overlapping images, or shimmering. May be subtle. Present in one eye only.

Binocular Diplopia: Discrete, separate images. Can be horizontal (medial/lateral rectus, CN VI palsy), vertical (superior/inferior rectus, CN III/IV palsy), or oblique. Worse in certain gaze directions. Disappears with head tilt or turn, or occlusion of one eye.

Associated Symptoms: Pain (orbital, retro-orbital, headache), Nausea/dizziness, Ptosis (CN III palsy, MG), Pupil abnormalities (CN III palsy), Proptosis (Graves', orbital mass), Dry eye symptoms, Ocular irritation.
Temporal Course: Acute onset (suggests urgent evaluation), chronic, intermittent, progressive, or fluctuating (Myasthenia Gravis).

sections.title: 7. Ocular Examination Findings
content: Visual Acuity & Refraction: Evaluate for uncorrected refractive error, astigmatism. Pin-hole test.
Pupillary Exam: Size, symmetry, reactivity (presence of anisocoria, relative afferent pupillary defect). Critical for CN III palsy.

Ocular Motility: Hirschberg test, Cover/Uncover, Alternate Cover Test to detect phorias/tropias. Evaluation of ductions and versions in all nine gaze positions. Saccades, pursuits, vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR).
Forced Duction Test: Differentiates restrictive vs. paretic strabismus (positive in restriction).
Hess Screen / Lancaster Red-Green Test: Quantifies ocular deviation in various gaze positions, identifies paretic muscle and overacting antagonists.
Slit-lamp Biomicroscopy: Corneal irregularities, cataract (location, density), IOL position/tilt, anterior chamber reaction.
Fundoscopy: Macular pathology (epiretinal membrane, edema), optic disc appearance.
Orbital Exam: Proptosis, lid lag, lid retraction (Graves'), orbital masses, periorbital ecchymosis/edema.

sections.title: 8. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Pinhole Test - Determines if diplopia is monocular (improves) or binocular (persists).
Step 2: Comprehensive Ophthalmic Exam - As detailed in Section 7.
Step 3: Refraction - Corrects for refractive causes of monocular diplopia.

Step 4: Neuroimaging (Binocular Diplopia) - MRI Brain & Orbits with contrast (and fat suppression for orbits) is preferred. CT for acute trauma or suspicion of bony involvement. Lumbar puncture if CNS infection or demyelinating disease suspected.

Step 5: Blood Investigations (Binocular Diplopia) - HbA1c (diabetes), ESR/CRP (Giant Cell Arteritis, inflammatory), Thyroid Function Tests (TSH, T3, T4, TRAb, anti-TPO for Graves' ophthalmopathy), Acetylcholine Receptor Antibodies (AChR-Ab) and MuSK Antibodies (for Myasthenia Gravis), Lyme serology, ANA (autoimmune disorders), Glucose.
Step 6: Electrophysiology - Single-fiber electromyography (SFEMG) for Myasthenia Gravis (most sensitive).
Step 7: Neuro-ophthalmology Consultation - For complex or neurological binocular diplopia.

rows: Ptosis, dilated pupil (pupil-involving, suggests compression), exotropia, hypotropia, limited adduction, elevation, depression
Vertical/oblique diplopia, worse on downgaze and adduction, compensatory head tilt to opposite shoulder (Bielschowsky sign)
Horizontal diplopia, esotropia, worse on lateral gaze to affected side, limited abduction
Fluctuating diplopia, ptosis, fatigability with sustained gaze, variable deviation, often asymmetric, positive AChR-Ab, positive Tensilon test/ice pack test
Proptosis, lid lag, lid retraction, restrictive strabismus (often IR, MR), positive TRAb, TSH abnormalities, 'E-L-M-S' mnemonic for muscle involvement
Pain, inflammation, proptosis, restricted motility, systemic signs of infection/inflammation, imaging shows enlarged muscle/inflammation
History of trauma, periocular edema/ecchymosis, restriction (muscle entrapment, e.g., IR in floor fracture), enophthalmos
Associated neurological deficits (hemiparesis, sensory loss, ataxia, nystagmus), MRI findings, acute onset
Vertical gaze palsy (downward first), falls, bradykinesia, usually no diplopia until late stage or in specific variants
Esotropia, restrictive, often affects CN VI palsy, but forced duction is negative

sections.title: 10. Staging/Grading (Relevant to Underlying Causes)
content: For Diplopia itself: No direct staging system. Severity can be graded by impact on daily activities (e.g., 'interferes with reading', 'requires patching for driving').

For Thyroid Eye Disease (TED): NOSPECS classification (No signs/symptoms, Only signs, Soft tissue involvement, Proptosis, Extraocular muscle involvement (diplopia often here), Corneal involvement, Sight loss). Diplopia falls under 'E'.
For Myasthenia Gravis: Osserman classification (ocular, mild generalized, acute fulminant, severe generalized, late severe). Ocular MG is relevant here.

For Cataract: LOCS III (Lens Opacities Classification System III) for grading morphology (nuclear, cortical, posterior subcapsular) and severity, which correlates with visual symptoms like monocular diplopia.

sections.title: 11. Management & Treatment: Monocular Diplopia
content: Correct Refractive Error: Prescription of appropriate spectacles/contact lenses for astigmatism or other ametropias.
Cataract Surgery: Phacoemulsification with IOL implantation for visually significant cataracts. Ensure appropriate IOL power calculation and centration.
Corneal Treatments: Therapeutic contact lenses for irregular astigmatism (e.g., keratoconus). Corneal transplantation (PKP/DALK) for severe scarring. PRK/LASIK for refractive errors.
Dry Eye Management: Lubricating drops, punctal plugs, immunomodulators (cyclosporine, lifitegrast) to stabilize tear film.
IOL Exchange/Repositioning: For symptomatic IOL decentration or tilt causing monocular diplopia/dysphotopsia.

sections.title: 12. Management & Treatment: Binocular Diplopia
content: Step 1: Treat the Underlying Cause - Crucial! (e.g., systemic steroids for GCA, immunosuppressants for MG/orbital pseudotumor, prism therapy/surgical intervention for strabismus, thyroid management for TED).

Step 2: Symptomatic Relief (Temporary) - Patching (alternate eyes to prevent amblyopia in children, or preferred eye in adults for comfort), Fresnel prisms (temporary, available up to ~40Δ, can be applied to spectacle lenses).
Step 3: Permanent Optical Correction - Ground-in prisms (for stable, comitant deviations up to ~15-20Δ total, can be split between eyes).
Step 4: Botulinum Toxin Injection - Into an overacting antagonist muscle (e.g., medial rectus in CN VI palsy) for temporary correction or diagnostic aid. Lasts ~3-4 months.

Step 5: Strabismus Surgery - For stable, comitant or incomitant deviations after underlying cause is managed and deviation has stabilized (usually 6-12 months post-onset for paralytic strabismus). Procedures include recession, resection, transpositions, adjustable sutures.
Step 6: Ocular Prosthetics/Occlusion - For intractable diplopia, a frosted lens or occlusive contact lens can be used over one eye.

sections.title: 13. Surgical Techniques for Binocular Diplopia
content: Strabismus Surgery: Recession (weakening) or Resection (strengthening) of extraocular muscles. Transposition procedures (e.g., for CN VI palsy). Adjustable sutures for fine-tuning post-operatively. Goals: fuse in primary gaze, expand field of single vision.
Orbital Decompression: For severe proptosis and compressive optic neuropathy in Thyroid Eye Disease. Can indirectly improve muscle restriction if orbital volume is reduced.
Eyelid Surgery: For ptosis (e.g., levator advancement) or lid retraction (e.g., Müller's muscle recession, spacer grafts) associated with diplopia.
Cataract Surgery (Monocular): Phacoemulsification with appropriate IOL selection/placement.

sections.title: 14. Complications & Prognosis
content: Uncorrected Diplopia: Can lead to significant quality of life impairment, falls, difficulty with reading, driving, and work. In children, can lead to amblyopia if chronic.
Recurrence: Possible depending on underlying etiology (e.g., recurrent MG exacerbations, progressive TED).

Prognosis: Highly dependent on the underlying cause. Microvascular cranial nerve palsies often resolve spontaneously within 3-6 months. Diplopia from restrictive myopathy or chronic strabismus may require long-term management or surgery. Life-threatening causes (aneurysm, tumor) have graver prognoses if not promptly treated.

sections.title: 15. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: Acute onset painful diplopia with headache (Giant Cell Arteritis in elderly, Cavernous Sinus Syndrome)
New onset binocular diplopia with pupil involvement (especially dilated, non-reactive pupil) in CN III palsy (posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise)
Diplopia with associated neurological signs (hemiparesis, sensory loss, ataxia, speech/swallowing difficulties) - suggests brainstem stroke or tumor
Rapidly progressive proptosis, pain, and vision loss (orbital cellulitis, orbital apex syndrome)
Fluctuating diplopia and ptosis with systemic weakness, dysphagia, dysarthria (Myasthenia Gravis crisis)
Acute onset in children (rare, requires immediate evaluation for tumor, trauma, hydrocephalus)

content.explanation: Lateral Rectus is innervated by Cranial Nerve VI (Abducens). Superior Oblique is innervated by Cranial Nerve IV (Trochlear). All other extraocular muscles (Medial Rectus, Superior Rectus, Inferior Rectus, Inferior Oblique, Levator Palpebrae Superioris, and pupil constrictors) are innervated by Cranial Nerve III (Oculomotor). Essential for localizing binocular diplopia due to cranial nerve palsies.

sections.title: 17. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always start by asking: 'Does the double vision go away if you cover one eye?' This immediately distinguishes monocular from binocular diplopia.
Pinhole test is your simplest, quickest diagnostic tool for monocular diplopia. If it improves, it's refractive or optical.
Isolated CN IV palsy often presents with a compensatory head tilt to the opposite shoulder. Look for it!
Acute, painful CN III palsy with pupil involvement is an aneurysm until proven otherwise – urgent neuroimaging is mandatory.
Myasthenia Gravis often 'mimics' other conditions and can present with isolated ocular symptoms (ocular MG). Fatigue on sustained gaze is a hallmark.
In thyroid eye disease, the inferior rectus is most commonly affected, causing vertical diplopia and restriction of upgaze.
Never dismiss diplopia; it is a symptom that can indicate serious, vision, or life-threatening conditions.

sections.title: 18. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent advances in diplopia management include more refined strabismus surgical techniques with adjustable sutures, improved understanding and management of specific underlying etiologies (e.g., targeted immunosuppression for MG, newer biologics for TED), and enhanced neuroimaging modalities for earlier detection of neurological causes. The role of optical coherence tomography (OCT) has expanded for subtle macular causes of monocular diplopia, and diagnostic algorithms continue to be refined for timely and accurate diagnosis. Landmark studies continue to guide evidence-based treatment for conditions like Thyroid Eye Disease (e.g., EUGOGO guidelines) and Myasthenia Gravis (e.g., clinical trials on monoclonal antibodies like eculizumab, ravulizumab).
